Indonesia has an overall safety risk rated as medium. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is medium. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Reissued after periodic review with minor edits.
Exercise increased caution in Indonesia due to terrorism and natural disasters. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.
Do Not travel to:

The provinces of Central Papua (Papua Tengah) and Highland Papua (Papua Pegunungan) due to civil unrest.

Country Summary: Terrorists continue plotting possible attacks in Indonesia. Terrorists may attack with little or no warning, targeting police stations, places of worship, hotels, b For solo female travelers: Exercise increased caution. Dress modestly outside tourist areas. Harassment can occur. Avoid traveling alone at night in less-touristed areas.. LGBTQ+ safety: Homosexuality is not illegal at the federal level but is banned in Aceh (under Sharia law). Climate is increasingly hostile — avoid public affection. Bali is relatively tolerant but not openly LGBTQ+ friendly.. Natural disaster risks include: earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, flooding, tropical storms.
In Indonesia, call 110 for police, 118 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 113 for fire services.  The U.S. Embassy Jakarta in Jakarta can be reached at +62-21-3435-9000.

Indonesia has a Mixed public-private (BPJS Kesehatan for residents) healthcare system, rated moderate quality. Typical costs for tourists: System: Mixed public-private (BPJS Kesehatan for residents) Quality: ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Healthcare quality varies significantly. Bali has good private international clinics and hospitals with English-speaking staff (BIMC, Sanglah public hospital). Java (Jakarta) has excellent international hospitals. Rural islands have very limited healthcare. Medical evacuation to Singapore or Australia may be necessary for serious conditions. 💡 Medical Tourism Indonesia is not typically a medical tourism destination for Westerners — rather, locals sometimes travel OUT for medical care. Bali does attract 'wellness tourists' for spa, yoga, and detox retreats.. Pharmacy access: easy. Access: easy Hours: Pharmacies (apotek) are common in Bali and major cities, typically open 9am-9pm. Some 24/7 pharmacies exist in larger cities. In smaller islands, pharmacy access is limited. Prescription rules: Many medications available OTC. For prescription medications, a local doctor's prescription may be required. International prescriptions are generally not accepted. Counterfeit medications are a real risk — use reputable pharmacies. 💡 Tips Many common medications are available without prescription, including antibiotics. However, quality can be inconsistent and counterfeit medications are a concern. Buy from reputable pharmacies (Kimia Farma, Guardian, or international clinics) when possible. Bring all prescription medications you may need. Recommended vaccinations: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (for rural Java/Bali), Rabies (for animal contact — Bali has rabies), COVID-19 (following current guidelines). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: ⚠️ Strongly recommended Average cost: $25-50/week 💡 Tip Medical evacuation from Bali to Singapore (3-4 hours) or Australia is often necessary for serious conditions. Ensure your insurance covers emergency evacuation. International clinics in Bali (especially in Seminyak, Ubud, Sanur) have direct billing with major insurers. 💡 Tip Medical evacuation from Bali to Singapore (3-4 hours) or Australia is often necessary for serious conditions. Ensure your insurance covers emergency evacuation. International clinics in Bali (especially in Seminyak, Ubud, Sanur) have direct billing with major insurers.

Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Indonesia. Legal with prescription under Indonesian pharmaceutical law. However, Indonesia has extremely strict drug enforcement—carry full documentation including doctor's letter.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Indonesia. Amphetamines are Category I narcotics under Law No. 35/2009. Possession carries mandatory prison sentences (4-12 years). Adderall is not available. Do NOT bring into Indonesia.

Cannabis / CBD is banned in Indonesia. Strictly illegal. Cannabis is a Category I narcotic. Penalties range from 4 years to life imprisonment; trafficking can carry the death penalty. CBD products are also illegal.

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Indonesia. Available by prescription from Indonesian doctors but tightly controlled. Importing personal supplies requires prior approval from BPOM (national drug authority). Carry full documentation.
Codeine / opioids is restricted in Indonesia. Codeine-containing medications require prescription. Stronger opioids are Category II narcotics with severe penalties for unauthorized possession.

Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is restricted in Indonesia. Controlled as a precursor substance. Available in limited formulations from pharmacies. Importing large quantities can trigger precursor trafficking charges.
Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Indonesia. Both are Category I narcotics. MDMA possession can result in 4-12 years imprisonment. Trafficking penalties include life imprisonment or death.
Tramadol is restricted in Indonesia. Prescription required. Has been subject to increasing regulation due to abuse concerns. Carry original packaging and prescription.

Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Indonesia. Available by prescription. Classified as psychotropic substance. Must have valid prescription; unauthorized possession is a criminal offense.

Cambodia has an overall safety risk rated as medium. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is medium. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased caution in Cambodia due to crime, civil unrest, and unexploded ordnance (UXO) in rural areas. Land mines remain a risk in remote areas near the Thai border. For solo female travelers: Exercise caution, especially at night. Avoid walking alone after dark in cities. Bag snatching from motorbikes is common. Dress modestly to reduce unwanted attention.. LGBTQ+ safety: Same-sex relationships are not criminalized but LGBTQ+ rights are limited. Public displays of affection by same-sex couples may attract negative attention in conservative areas.. Natural disaster risks include: flooding, tropical storms, drought, unexploded ordnance (UXO).

In Cambodia, call 117 for police, 119 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 118 for fire services. Emergency services can be slow outside Phnom Penh. English-speaking operators rare — hotel staff can assist. Tourist Police: +855-23-724-793. The U.S. Embassy Phnom Penh in Phnom Penh can be reached at +855-23-728-000.

Cambodia has a Underdeveloped public system; private hospitals in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap recommended for tourists healthcare system, rated poor quality. Typical costs for tourists: Private clinic visit $30-80. Emergency care at international clinics $100-400. Serious conditions require evacuation to Bangkok (approx. $15,000-50,000). Hospital stay at private facilities $200-600/night.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies common in cities. Quality varies — counterfeit medications exist. Stick to reputable pharmacies in tourist areas.. Calmette Hospital and Royal Phnom Penh Hospital serve emergencies. For serious conditions, medical evacuation to Bangkok or Singapore is strongly recommended. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis, Rabies, COVID-19. Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: Comprehensive travel insurance including emergency medical evacuation is essential. Medical facilities outside Phnom Penh are severely limited.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Cambodia. Technically prescription-only but widely available OTC in pharmacies; travelers should still carry prescription for border crossings
Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Cambodia. Amphetamines (yaba/ice) are major enforcement targets; Adderall is banned. Severe penalties including life imprisonment
Cannabis / CBD is banned in Cambodia. Illegal under 2012 Drug Control Law despite historical use; penalties include imprisonment. CBD status unclear—avoid
Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Cambodia. Controlled psychotropic; not commonly prescribed in Cambodia. Carry full documentation if importing personal supply
Codeine / opioids is restricted in Cambodia. Available in some pharmacies without strict controls in practice, but legally requires prescription. Keep original packaging
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is caution in Cambodia. Controlled as methamphetamine precursor but enforcement varies; carry in original packaging with receipt
Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Cambodia. Illegal under Cambodian drug law; despite 'happy pizza' tourism reputation, penalties are severe if caught formally
Tramadol is restricted in Cambodia. Available in pharmacies but legally controlled; carry prescription documentation when entering the country
Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Cambodia. Controlled substance; available at pharmacies but carry prescription for legal protection at border

Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Singapore. Class C controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act. Legal with valid prescription. Travelers may bring up to 3 months' supply with doctor's letter and original packaging. HSA approval needed for larger quantities.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Singapore. Amphetamines are Class A controlled drugs — the most serious category. Adderall is completely banned. Importing ANY quantity can result in severe penalties including caning and lengthy imprisonment. Death penalty applies for trafficking (>15g).

Cannabis / CBD is banned in Singapore. Strictly banned. Cannabis is Class A. CBD products are also prohibited regardless of THC content. Trafficking >500g carries mandatory death penalty. Even trace amounts in urine can lead to charges.

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Singapore. Class B controlled drug. Available by prescription in Singapore. Travelers must carry valid prescription, doctor's letter, and keep in original packaging. Declare at customs for quantities exceeding personal use.

Codeine / opioids is restricted in Singapore. Codeine at low doses is available OTC in some preparations. Stronger opioids are Class A controlled drugs. Travelers should carry prescriptions and keep medications in original packaging. Morphine trafficking >30g carries death penalty.

Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is restricted in Singapore. Available in pharmacies with ID registration. Not a controlled drug but regulated as a precursor. Travelers may bring personal supply in original packaging without special permit.

Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Singapore. Both are Class A controlled drugs. Severe penalties including lengthy imprisonment and caning. MDMA trafficking carries potential death penalty. Absolutely zero tolerance.
Tramadol is restricted in Singapore. Prescription-only controlled substance. Travelers may bring personal supply with valid prescription and doctor's letter. Keep in original pharmacy packaging.

Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Singapore. Prescription-only medication. Travelers may bring personal supply (up to 3 months) with valid prescription. Must be in original packaging with pharmacy label.

Thailand has an overall safety risk rated as low. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is moderate. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased caution in Thailand due to risk of unrest. Some areas have increased risk. Violent crime is rare against tourists but does occur. For solo female travelers: Generally safe. Exercise normal caution at night, especially on islands and in nightlife areas. Drink spiking occurs — watch your drinks. Full moon parties on Koh Phangan require extra vigilance.. LGBTQ+ safety: Very tolerant culturally. Thailand is one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries in Asia. Same-sex marriage legalized in 2024. Bangkok has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Kathoey (transgender women) are culturally visible.. Natural disaster risks include: flooding (monsoon season), tsunamis (Andaman coast), earthquakes (northern region).

In Thailand, call 191 for police, 1669 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 199 for fire services. Tourist police: 1155 (English-speaking, available 24/7). This should be your first call for non-emergency issues. The U.S. Embassy Bangkok in Bangkok can be reached at +66-2-205-4000.

Thailand has a Mixed public/private healthcare system, rated good quality. Typical costs for tourists: Private hospitals cater to medical tourists and are excellent quality. Clinic visit $30-80. Emergency room $100-500. Private hospital stay $150-500/night. Bumrungrad International Hospital (Bangkok) is world-class. Public hospitals are cheaper ($10-50) but crowded with long waits and limited English.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies are everywhere and many medications available OTC that require prescriptions in Western countries — including some antibiotics and pain medications. Pharmacists often speak basic English.. Bangkok has world-class private hospitals (Bumrungrad, Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej) popular with medical tourists. Outside Bangkok, quality drops significantly. Chiang Mai has adequate private hospitals. Islands and rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Bangkok. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (if rural), Rabies (if rural/animal contact). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: Travel insurance essential. Private hospitals require proof of insurance or cash deposit upfront ($500-2,000). Medevac coverage strongly recommended if visiting islands or rural areas.
Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Thailand. Strictly illegal. Thailand has severe drug penalties including long prison sentences. No exemption for foreign prescriptions.
CBD / cannabis products is restricted in Thailand. Cannabis was re-criminalized in 2025. CBD products with >0.2% THC are illegal. Enforcement is increasing. Do not bring any cannabis products.
Codeine is restricted in Thailand. Controlled substance. Bring prescription documentation and keep in original packaging. Maximum 30 days supply.
Tramadol is restricted in Thailand. Classified as a narcotic. Bring doctor's letter and original prescription. Keep in original packaging.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Thailand. Psychotropic substances requiring documentation. Carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Max 30-day supply.

Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Vietnam. Available by prescription. Classified as psychotropic substances under Vietnam's drug control laws. Carry original packaging and doctor's documentation—Vietnam has strict drug enforcement.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Vietnam. Amphetamines are strictly illegal narcotics in Vietnam. Penalties are among the harshest in the world—possession of >100g of amphetamines can carry the death penalty. Adderall is not available. Do NOT bring into Vietnam.

Cannabis / CBD is banned in Vietnam. Cannabis is strictly illegal in all forms. Possession can result in 1-5 years imprisonment; trafficking of large quantities can carry the death penalty. CBD products are also illegal.

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Vietnam. Limited availability. Classified as psychotropic substance under Decree 73/2018. Requires prescription and documentation. Travelers should carry a doctor's letter and prior authorization may be needed.

Codeine / opioids is restricted in Vietnam. Codeine requires prescription. Opioids strictly controlled—heroin trafficking carries the death penalty. Even prescription opioids require careful documentation. Carry original packaging and medical records.

Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is restricted in Vietnam. Controlled as a precursor chemical under Vietnamese law. Regulated by Ministry of Health. Available in limited pharmaceutical formulations with restrictions.
Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Vietnam. Both are illegal narcotics. Vietnam has some of the world's strictest drug penalties. MDMA trafficking can carry life imprisonment or the death penalty.
Tramadol is restricted in Vietnam. Prescription required. Added to Vietnam's controlled substances list. Carry original packaging and full medical documentation.

Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Vietnam. Available by prescription. Classified as psychotropic substance. Must have valid prescription and original packaging. Unauthorized possession is a criminal offense.
