For older travelers on a Vietnam guided tour or independent trip, the defense: (1) book ONLY via Bhaya Classic, Paradise Elegance, Heritage Bình Chuẩn, Orchid, Indochina Sails, Emperor Cruises, or Stellar of the Seas — all well-established and independently-reviewed; (2) verify the URL exactly (bhayacruises.com, paradisevietnam.com, emperorcruises.com) — clone sites use variations; (3) pay by credit card only — never wire transfer, Bizum, or cryptocurrency; (4) compare the price to recent 2024–2025 TripAdvisor and Reddit reports — typical 2-day/1-night cruise is $150–$250 per person; anything under $80 is a scam or deeply-deficient operator; (5) verify the booking a week ahead by calling the operator directly. How to avoid: Book ONLY via well-established operators: Bhaya, Paradise, Heritage, Orchid, Indochina Sails, Emperor Verify the operator domain exactly — type the URL manually, never click Google ads Pay by credit card only — refuse wire transfer, Bizum, or cryptocurrency payment Expect $150–$250 per person for 2-day/1-night; anything under $80 is scam-tier Verify the booking by phone to the operator a week before arrival

Scam alert in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam — Hanoi-to-Ha Long Shuttle Bus & Private Transfer Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). The 3.5–4-hour drive between Hanoi and Ha Long (Tuan Chau or Ha Long City) has generated a distinct transfer-overcharge scam. The legitimate shuttle-bus rate is 300,000–500,000 VND per person (round trip, shared bus, ~$12–$20); private car transfers are 2,500,000–4,000,000 VND total (one-way, ~$100–$160). Scammers at Hanoi Old Quarter 'tourist offices' quote 'cruise + shuttle' packages at 5–10x the legitimate component rates and often book via 'partner' shuttle operators that are low-quality or don't actually connect with the cruise departure time. One traveler wrote: 'Booked a ha long bay cruise at an office in Ha Noi, got scammed, now he threatened to send someone' after the victim tried to dispute. Community reports document the Ha Long-end return-ride overcharge pattern, and travelers describe being quoted 3x the legitimate rate by Old Quarter offices for a shared shuttle bus. The 'Sinh Tourist' copycat problem is severe — there are multiple storefronts using 'Sinh' in their names but only one legitimate operator (The Sinh Tourist, thesinhtourist.vn, founded 1993). Community reports also warn about the broader booking-website fraud ecosystem affecting all Vietnam intercity transfers. For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) book the shuttle through your cruise operator directly — most cruises include transfers in the package price; (2) if booking independently, use The Sinh Tourist (thesinhtourist.vn, verify URL exactly) or Hanoi Transfer Service; (3) for private car, pre-book via Klook, 12Go Asia, or direct with a licensed operator at $100–$160 one-way; (4) avoid any Old Quarter 'tourist office' quoting 'special deals'; (5) for the return from Ha Long, use the cruise operator's return shuttle or pre-book a Grab for Ha Long City to the Hanoi drop-off point; (6) expect ~4 hours one-way; if 'faster routes' are advertised, they don't exist. How to avoid: Book shuttle through your cruise operator directly — most include transfers in package price For independent booking, use The Sinh Tourist (thesinhtourist.vn — verify URL exactly) or Hanoi Transfer Service Pre-book private car via Klook, 12Go Asia, or licensed operator at $100–$160 one-way Avoid Old Quarter 'tourist offices' quoting 'special deals' — all are aggregators with markup For Ha Long return, use cruise-operator shuttle or pre-book Grab for Ha Long City

Scam alert in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam — Onboard Ha Long Cruise Upcharges & 'Mandatory' Activity Fees (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Even on a legitimate cruise, Ha Long operators generate revenue through onboard upcharges that aren't clearly disclosed at booking. The common genres: (1) 'kayaking' advertised as included but actually requiring a 300,000–500,000 VND 'supplement' once onboard; (2) professional photographer 'included' for free but the USB drive of photos costs 2,000,000+ VND; (3) 'welcome cocktail' leads to a bottle-service upsell; (4) 'wine pairing dinner' at 800,000 VND per person above the package; (5) 'premium cabin upgrade' offered at arrival when your originally-booked cabin is 'unfortunately unavailable.' Community reviews document specific onboard pressure patterns. Travelers capture the overall frustration: 'every review of Ha Long Bay says its terrible... 4 days is not enough in ha long at all. Cruise side is called Tuan Chau. Bai Chay is the beach side.' Reports also document differentiation between cruise operators: 'Our boat was quiet and peaceful but others did have more of a party vibe so probably worth checking' before booking. For older travelers on a cruise, the defense: (1) read the FULL itinerary including activity list at booking — kayaking should be explicit as 'included' or 'optional supplement'; (2) photograph the package breakdown from the confirmation email so you can dispute onboard charges; (3) decline all onboard upsells politely — 'we'll take pictures ourselves'; (4) if offered a 'cabin upgrade' at arrival, politely decline and insist on the originally booked cabin — the 'unavailable' claim is a pressure tactic; (5) bring your own snorkel/reading material rather than buying onboard; (6) check the final bill item-by-item before settling. How to avoid: Read the FULL itinerary before booking — activities labelled 'included' vs 'optional supplement' Photograph the package breakdown from confirmation email for onboard dispute reference Decline all onboard upsells politely — take your own photos, bring your own snorkel If offered 'cabin upgrade' at arrival, insist on originally booked cabin — claim is pressure tactic Check final bill item-by-item before settling the account

Scam alert in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam — Fake 'Floating Village' Tour & Diesel-Sampan Swap (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Ha Long Bay's 'floating villages' are a distinctive photo-op that cruise operators advertise heavily — but the reality of what tourists encounter has shifted significantly. A former Ha Long Bay tour guide wrote: 'I worked as a tour guide in Halong Bay for 3 months. There is no floating village in the way tourists expect' — what exists are small fishing settlements that are partially abandoned due to environmental-protection relocation, and several 'reconstructed floating villages' built specifically as photo stops for tourist cruises. Travelers add the operational warning: 'Those fake sampan boats are filthy, spewing diesel into the water. The tours are run by hustlers who swap out the advertised "traditional rowing" sampan for a diesel motor sampan halfway through.' The scam pattern: a cruise advertises 'authentic floating-village visit' and 'silent traditional sampan experience'; in practice, tourists are transferred to a diesel-powered sampan with a loud motor, visit a 'reconstructed village' that is mostly a commercial souvenir stop, and are pressured to buy pearls, dried squid, or 'local' handicrafts at 3–5x market prices. Community reports reflect broader Vietnamese tourist-trap fatigue and document the Cat Ba-specific alternative. For older travelers on a Ha Long cruise, the practical rule: (1) accept that 'floating village' visits are commercial photo stops — do not buy pearls, squid, or handicrafts from onboard vendors; (2) request the Lan Ha Bay route (off Cat Ba Island) instead of the main Ha Long Bay tourist route — fewer cruise ships, more authentic kayak experiences; (3) for the kayaking portion, use the life jackets provided (no matter your swim ability — Ha Long waters have currents); (4) the 'photo package' offered onboard can cost 2M+ VND — take your own photos; (5) genuine pearls are expensive even in Vietnam; onboard 'pearl farm' visits selling $30 pearl necklaces are selling freshwater paste-pearls or plastic. How to avoid: Accept 'floating village' visits are commercial photo stops — do not buy from onboard vendors Request Lan Ha Bay route (Cat Ba) instead of Ha Long Bay main — fewer ships, more authentic Use life jackets during kayaking regardless of swim ability (currents are real) Take your own photos — 'photo package' can cost 2M+ VND Don't buy 'pearls' onboard — genuine Vietnamese pearls are expensive; $30 necklaces are paste/plastic

Scam alert in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam — Ha Long City / Tuan Chau Pier Street Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Once cruise passengers disembark at Tuan Chau or Ha Long City, the return-taxi economy runs on the same meter-tampering and fixed-price patterns as Hanoi but with a smaller supply of legitimate operators. The legitimate taxi fare from Tuan Chau Pier to Ha Long City Bai Chay (or vice versa) is 100,000–150,000 VND; to local hotels 50,000–100,000 VND. Community reports document the Ha Long-end overcharge pattern. Travelers describe the town: 'It's a lovely town, really beautiful, but very quiet. In the day you can walk the sea front' — the town's small size means taxi supply is limited and scammers exploit that. The scam patterns: (1) driver claims the meter is 'broken' and quotes 'fixed' 500,000–800,000 VND for 3-km pier trips; (2) driver takes winding routes to inflate metered distance; (3) night rates invoked during day hours; (4) 'luggage supplement' demanded on top of fare; (5) driver claims the agreed price was 'per person' rather than per trip. For cruise passengers disembarking for a post-cruise Ha Long City visit, the practical defense: (1) pre-arrange cruise-operator return-shuttle if included; (2) use Grab app if available (coverage is spotty in Ha Long); (3) for licensed taxi, use Mai Linh or Taxi Group — verify company phone number matches the company website; (4) confirm approximate fare before boarding (100K–150K VND Tuan Chau-Bai Chay); (5) photograph the taxi plate number from the rear windscreen; (6) for the transfer back to Hanoi, use the cruise-operator shuttle or pre-book a return private car rather than hailing at the pier. How to avoid: Pre-arrange cruise-operator return shuttle if included in package Use Grab app if coverage available (spotty in Ha Long area) For street taxi, use only Mai Linh or Taxi Group — verify company phone number on door Confirm approximate fare before boarding: 100K–150K VND Tuan Chau-Bai Chay, 50K–100K VND local hotel Photograph taxi plate number from rear windscreen on entering

Scam alert in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam — Booking.com / Agoda Off-Platform Payment Fraud for Ha Long Cruises (tourist-trap, severity: high). A specific 2025 scam targets Ha Long Bay cruise bookings made through platforms like Booking.com and Agoda. After a legitimate booking, a fake 'host' or 'cruise operator' contacts the traveler via WhatsApp or email claiming 'payment verification issues' and requesting an additional off-platform transfer (Bizum, bank transfer, cryptocurrency, or a payment link that is actually phishing). Travelers document the pattern: 'Pretty common scam. If you get a message from Agoda or Booking with a link to a different site, ignore it. Your booking is either complete as-is or the platform will charge the card on file at the property.' 2025 reports confirm the Agoda variant, and community reports document the Booking.com-wide platform-impersonation pattern that specifically targets Ha Long Bay cruises. The scam sophistication: messages include correct booking reference numbers (because scammers are pulling from leaked platform data), correct cruise names, and correct dates — the only giveaway is the request for off-platform payment. For older travelers on a pre-booked Ha Long cruise, the defense: (1) ANY message requesting additional payment off-platform is a scam — legitimate operators collect payment at the pier or through the platform's card-on-file system; (2) if you receive a WhatsApp or email claiming 'verification issues,' contact Booking.com or Agoda support directly via the app — never click links in the message; (3) refuse all Bizum, Western Union, cryptocurrency, or unfamiliar-gateway payment requests; (4) verify cruise bookings a week before arrival by calling the operator from a number found on the official operator website (not the number in the email); (5) if defrauded, file a chargeback with your credit card immediately and report to Booking.com/Agoda fraud channels. How to avoid: Treat ANY off-platform payment request as a scam — legitimate bookings collect at pier or via card-on-file If you receive 'verification' message, contact Booking.com or Agoda support via the APP — never click message links Refuse Bizum, Western Union, cryptocurrency, or unfamiliar-gateway payment requests Verify cruise bookings a week before arrival by calling the operator from their OFFICIAL website number If defrauded, file credit card chargeback immediately and report to platform fraud channels

Scam alert in Hanoi, Vietnam — Hanoi Noi Bai Airport (HAN) Fake-Grab Driver Scam (transport, severity: high). How to avoid: NEVER accept 'free tour' or 'friendly local' motorbike offers — all escalate to 1.5M+ VND Use GrabBike or Be Bike app for short rides — app-regulated fares, GPS tracked For guided motorbike tours, book via Vespa Adventures, Hanoi Backstreet Tours, or Hanoi Vespa Tour Older travelers: consider walking tours or small-group car tours rather than motorbike Reject any ride without a helmet for the passenger — legal requirement in Vietnam

Community reports document the May 2023 policy change: a new fee to enter Hoi An starting May 15 — the 120,000 VND (adult) / 80,000 VND (combined with monuments) ticket is now required for tourists entering the Ancient Town perimeter, not just the monuments themselves. Travelers note the scope: the ticket is to enter the old streets and some special monumental places; the money funds heritage preservation. The scam variants that have emerged: (1) unofficial 'ticket checkers' at secondary entry points demanding cash for tickets already purchased; (2) 'combo ticket' touts outside the official booth selling 3x-markup tickets with 'extra access' claims that don't exist; (3) confusion about which monuments your ticket covers (it covers 5 of your choice, not all); (4) entry through back alleys attempted to avoid the fee — but checkers now patrol these routes. Community reports add context about the monthly full-moon festival where street lights are turned off for lantern evenings — the Ancient Town ticket covers this too. For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) buy Ancient Town tickets at OFFICIAL booths at main entrance points — 120,000 VND adults (2025); the ticket gives access to 5 monuments of your choice from a list of 20+; (2) plan your 5-monument choice: Japanese Covered Bridge, Phung Hung Ancient House, Hai Nan Assembly Hall, Tran Family Chapel, Quan Cong Temple are most community-recommended; (3) keep your ticket visible when walking the Ancient Town — checkers occasionally verify; (4) REFUSE 'ticket checkers' demanding additional cash if you already have a ticket; (5) for older travelers with mobility concerns, the Ancient Town is walkable in 3–4 hours with 2–3 monument stops plus lunch; (6) the 'full moon festival' (monthly, 14th day of lunar month) is free with your Ancient Town ticket — no additional fee. How to avoid: Buy at OFFICIAL booths at main Ancient Town entrance — 120K VND adults (2025) Plan 5-monument choice: Japanese Covered Bridge, Phung Hung, Hai Nan Hall, Tran Family, Quan Cong Keep ticket visible when walking Ancient Town — checkers occasionally verify REFUSE 'ticket checkers' demanding additional cash if you already have a ticket Full-moon festival is FREE with Ancient Town ticket — no additional fee

Scam alert in Hoi An, Vietnam — Hoi An 'Fruit Ladies' Photo Trap & Forced Weight Overcharge (tourist-trap, severity: minor). A specific 2025 Hoi An scam targets tourists seeking 'authentic' photos of Vietnamese women carrying bamboo poles with fruit baskets (gánh hàng rong). Community reports.' The scam sequence: (1) a woman in traditional dress with fruit baskets positions herself at a photogenic corner; (2) she offers to let tourists 'try on the hat and baskets for a photo'; (3) once the photo is taken, she demands payment — typically 200K–500K VND, sometimes with 'forced purchase' of fruit at 100K VND for what should cost 10K; (4) if the tourist refuses, she becomes loud and attracts a crowd, escalating social pressure. Travelers describe the related English-speaker approach pattern: 'After living in Vietnam, if anyone approaches you and speaks English well, it's a scam or commissioned tout operation.' One 2025 traveler captured broader sentiment: 'Out of all of that, Hoi An was our least favorite. Feels like the motto is: cram them in and extract every dong.' The fruit-lady scam is part of a broader commercialisation pattern where every photo opportunity has been monetised. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) NEVER accept offers to 'try on' a fruit-basket hat or pose with a stranger's props for a photo; (2) if you want an 'authentic' photo, politely ask from a distance WITHOUT touching props — agree a price (typically 20K–50K VND) before taking the photo; (3) buy fruit ONLY from fixed-stall vendors with posted-price signs, not from mobile fruit-lady carts; (4) typical fruit prices: 20K VND for a pineapple, 30K for 500g rambutan, 40K for a dragon fruit; (5) if caught in a photo-demand, pay 50K VND maximum (already above fair rate) and walk away — scammers rarely escalate beyond shouting; (6) document the experience on travel community forums so others are warned. How to avoid: NEVER try on a fruit-basket hat or pose with stranger's props For 'authentic' photos, politely ask from a distance WITHOUT touching — agree 20K–50K VND before photo Buy fruit ONLY from fixed-stall vendors with posted prices (20K pineapple, 30K rambutan 500g) If caught in a photo-demand, pay 50K VND maximum and walk away Scammers rarely escalate beyond shouting — don't let crowd pressure coerce you

Scam alert in Hoi An, Vietnam — Hoi An Cooking Class / Tour Booking Kickback Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hoi An's cooking-class economy and Cham Island/My Son day-trip bookings have a specific kickback-and-overcharge pattern. Community reports document the pattern: 'We took tours and attended cooking classes. Scam after scam' — kickback-driven recommendations from hotels and touts inflate prices 30–100% above direct-booking rates. 2025 reports capture the overcrowding context, describing Hoi An as 'cram them in' — commercialised tour volume amplifies kickback opportunities. Community reports also document generic-tour-operator issues that apply in Hoi An. The scam variants: (1) hotel concierge recommends 'partner' cooking class at $50/person when the direct-booking rate at the same venue is $30/person; (2) tout at Ancient Town offers 'discount cooking class' at $35 but it's a lower-quality operator than advertised; (3) 'day trip to My Son temples' quoted at $60 per person via hotel when Klook/GetYourGuide direct is $25; (4) 'Cham Island snorkelling day trip' at $80 via tout when direct is $45; (5) online bookings via unfamiliar aggregators that upcharge 50%. For older travelers considering a Hoi An cooking class or day tour, the protective playbook: (1) book cooking classes directly via the venue's own website — community-recommended: Red Bridge Cooking School (redbridgecookingschool.com), Morning Glory Cooking School (facebook.com/morningglorycooking), Vy's Market Restaurant Cooking Class; expect $25–$40 per person for 4-hour class including market visit; (2) for My Son temples, book via Klook/GetYourGuide at $20–$30 — half-day tour including guide; (3) for Cham Island snorkelling, book via Klook or direct at the An Bang Beach jetty at $40–$55 per person; (4) REFUSE hotel 'partner' recommendations and Ancient Town touts; (5) verify any online booking is via a platform with cancellation protection (Klook, GetYourGuide, Viator) — never wire transfer. How to avoid: Book cooking classes DIRECT: Red Bridge, Morning Glory, Vy's Market ($25–$40/person) For My Son temples, book via Klook/GetYourGuide ($20–$30 half-day) For Cham Island snorkelling, book Klook or An Bang jetty direct ($40–$55) REFUSE hotel 'partner' recommendations and Ancient Town touts Only use platforms with cancellation protection (Klook, GetYourGuide, Viator) — never wire transfer

Scam alert in Hoi An, Vietnam — Hoi An Beach Bicycle & Motorbike Rental Damage Claims (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hoi An's bike-rental economy serves the daily commute to An Bang Beach (5 km east of Ancient Town). The scam: rental shops take a 'deposit' (cash, passport, or both) and at return claim minor scratches or tyre issues to retain the deposit. Community reports capture the broader 2025 pattern: rental + police shakedown combinations are documented. The scam variants: (1) bicycle rental shop takes 200K VND deposit, claims 'scratch damage' at return demanding 150K+ VND; (2) passport taken as deposit and withheld until additional 'cleaning fee' is paid; (3) motorbike rental at $5–$10/day shop claims 'helmet damage' or 'fuel shortage' at return; (4) hotel-provided 'free bicycles' charged 300K+ VND at checkout for 'damage' that wasn't documented. Travelers note a Southeast Asia-wide passport-deposit debate: 'Every time we travel to the islands in Thailand they take passports as deposit' — but the cross-Asia concern about passport-retention is real in Hoi An too. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) use hotel-provided bicycles where possible — most 3-4 star Hoi An hotels include bikes free with the stay; (2) if renting independently, use established operators (Mr. Hai, The Pedal Collective, Long Life Bikes) with clear written policies; (3) NEVER leave your passport as a deposit — offer cash deposit only (200K VND is standard); (4) photograph the bike from all angles BEFORE riding away; (5) for motorbikes, only use Motorvina/Tigit-quality operators with English paperwork; (6) at return, video the bike/motorbike showing no new damage; (7) if the shop claims damage you didn't cause, dispute with photographic evidence and contact Hoi An Tourist Police (Hoang Dieu Street, +84 235 3861 234) if escalated. How to avoid: Use hotel-provided bicycles where possible (most 3-4 star Hoi An hotels include them) For independent rental, use Mr. Hai, The Pedal Collective, or Long Life Bikes NEVER leave passport as deposit — cash deposit 200K VND is standard Photograph bike from all angles BEFORE riding away At return, video the bike showing no new damage

Scam alert in Hua Hin, Thailand — Hua Hin Taxi Mafia Threats & Grab Attacks (transport, severity: high). You book a Grab from your Hua Hin hotel to the train station. The Grab driver picks you up. A tuk-tuk driver nearby throws an egg at the Grab car window. Community reports document this exact aggressive enforcement: 'The taxi mafia there are terrible! I've both been aggressively threatened by a taxi driver and scammed (meter tampering).' Another traveler wrote: 'Similar situation happened a few weeks ago — it made the news. The taxi mafia were throwing eggs at a Grab car after picking up a customer.' Hua Hin's taxi cartel is more physically aggressive than most — other community reports mention 'taxi mafia in Hua Hin at the train station too.' How to avoid: Walk 200–300m away from the Hua Hin train station and Market Village before requesting Grab Pre-book hotel transfers via your accommodation for arrivals — fixed price in writing Benchmark Grab fares: Hua Hin town center → Khao Takiab ฿100, → railway station ฿80, → Cicada Market ฿120 For short in-town moves, walk or rent a bicycle at ฿100/day — Hua Hin is walkable Report egg-throwing or threatening incidents to Tourist Police 1155 with vehicle plate — these made news in 2025

Scam alert in Hua Hin, Thailand — Hua Hin Strip Club / Brothel Bill Extortion (nightlife, severity: high). You enter a Soi Bintabaht bar that a tout has recommended. A hostess sits down, drinks appear, and a 'bar fine' of ฿1,500 is added to take a girl off-shift. At the end of the night your bill is ฿15,000+ with line items you don't recognize. When you dispute, four men move between you and the door. Community reports document the pattern: a tourist in Thailand stands firm and refuses to pay his padded bill at a strip club/brothel that is infamous for such scams, and cowardly bouncers try to enforce payment. Hua Hin's nightlife scene is smaller than Pattaya's or Bangkok's Patpong, but the scam structure is identical — inflated bills, blocked exits, physical intimidation. How to avoid: Avoid any bar a street tout pulls you toward — this is the single most reliable scam indicator Pay for each drink individually at the bar — never a tab Carry ฿2,000 cash only, leave all cards and passports at the hotel Stick to bars with posted prices and Google Maps reviews (Monsoon Bar, Hilton rooftop, El Murphy's) If padded bill and exit blocked, call Tourist Police 1155 on speaker — venues fold at the police mention

Scam alert in Hua Hin, Thailand — Hua Hin Zoo & Attraction Dual Pricing (English Menu Markup) (overcharging, severity: low). At Hua Hin Zoo (Santorini Park area) you see a sign in Thai posting admission at ฿80 — but the English counter ticket reads ฿300. Beyond the government-sanctioned 10x foreigner pricing at national sites, many private Hua Hin attractions run informal dual pricing. One traveler wrote: 'At Hua Hin, like a zoo (back of Hua Hin), the price-list writing with the number in Thai is much cheaper than the price list in English' — meaning the Thai-language price board shows one number, the English one shows a different one, without any legal basis for the markup. How to avoid: Google attraction prices before arriving — Hua Hin Zoo real foreign admission is ฿350 as of 2025 Ask to see both English and Thai menus at restaurants; prices should match for same dishes Walk 2–3 blocks inland from Hua Hin beach for local-priced restaurants Cicada Market weekend vendors are near-fair priced; beachfront vendors are heavily marked up Use Google Maps reviews (4.3+ average, 100+ reviews) to filter out tourist-price traps

Scam alert in Hua Hin, Thailand — Hua Hin Property & Condo Agent Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Long-term tourists and expats in Hua Hin face a specialized scam: property agents selling condos they don't legally own, taking full cash payments, and disappearing. One traveler wrote: 'We bought a condo in Hua Hin a month ago and we paid all the money. Still not received the official blue book. Other people we know in Thailand keep saying it's very suspicious' — the 'blue book' (tabien baan) is the property ownership document; without it, you have no proof of purchase. Community reports also flag specific Hua Hin condo developments with systemic issues. How to avoid: Never pay cash upfront for property purchase — use an escrow lawyer (฿20,000–฿50,000 in fees is standard) Verify ownership at the Thai Land Department before paying any deposit For short-term (under 3 months), use Booking.com, Airbnb, or Agoda with credit card Verify agent license via Thai Real Estate Broker Association (treba.or.th) If scammed, file with Tourist Police 1155 immediately — 2025 enforcement actions have succeeded

Scam alert in Hua Hin, Thailand — Beach Jet Ski & Watersports Damage Shakedown (Lighter Variant) (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hua Hin Beach's jet ski rental scam is the less-famous cousin of Pattaya's and Phuket's — lower dollar amounts (฿5,000–฿15,000 damage claims rather than ฿30,000–฿300,000) but the same mechanics. Operators rent jet skis with pre-existing damage hidden under tape, 'discover' damage on return, and demand cash with a 'police' officer magically appearing to enforce. Community reports list Hua Hin alongside Pattaya and Samet as scam locations, and travelers note that the primary Thailand jet-ski rental scam pattern is well-documented with Hua Hin often mentioned in discussion. How to avoid: Do not rent jet skis, parasail, or banana boats from Hua Hin beach operators — the scam risk outweighs the experience If you want watersports, book through a licensed resort (Hua Hin Marriott, Hyatt Regency) with written insurance Photograph equipment before use with timestamps; refuse rental if no pre-inspection sheet is offered Pay by credit card where possible for chargeback leverage If targeted, refuse to pay on the spot and call Tourist Police 1155 (not the 'officer' on scene)

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Hue Cyclo Tourist Price & Mid-Ride Extortion (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hue's cyclo (pedal rickshaw) economy is a living tradition but has a documented tourist-overcharge and mid-ride extortion pattern. Community reports capture the baseline: 'It's a good experience where you can enjoy the street view, but it has become so expensive' for tourists specifically. Reports from Saigon document the broader Vietnam pattern that applies in Hue as well. The scam patterns in Hue: (1) cyclo driver quotes 50,000 VND at pickup, demands 500,000 VND at drop-off citing 'extra stops' or 'per-person pricing'; (2) driver stops mid-route at a 'friend's' shop (jewelry, lacquer, tailor) and pressures tourists to buy with kickback arrangement; (3) short 15-minute rides quoted at 200,000+ VND when the legitimate rate is 50,000–100,000 VND. Travelers capture the core issue: some commenters argue that charging foreigners a higher price is acceptable — this 'tourist tax' framing enables the scam ecosystem. The cyclo scam is one of the oldest Vietnamese tourist scams. For older travelers interested in the cyclo experience, the practical rule: (1) agree on TOTAL price (not per-person) in writing or on a clear phone-note before boarding; (2) expected rate: 50,000–100,000 VND for 15–30 minutes, 200,000 VND for 1 hour; (3) refuse any mid-route 'friend's shop' detour — insist on the agreed destination; (4) carry exact change in small notes; (5) for older travelers less comfortable negotiating, book via hotel (hotel arranges flat-rate cyclo at 150,000–250,000 VND per 30 min); (6) alternatively, use Grab bike (GrabBike) for 30,000–50,000 VND short rides — app-regulated, no negotiation required. How to avoid: Agree TOTAL price (not per person) in writing or phone note before boarding Expected rate: 50K–100K VND for 15–30 min, 200K VND for 1 hour Refuse mid-route 'friend's shop' detours — insist on agreed destination For older travelers, book via hotel for flat-rate (150K–250K VND per 30 min) Alternative: use GrabBike app for 30K–50K VND short rides

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Hue Grab & Taxi 700,000 VND Airport Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Hue has a documented 2025 airport-taxi overcharge pattern. One traveler wrote: 'Total scam outfit at Hue. Drivers asking 700k to get to downtown. I walked 2km away from the arrivals hall to book a legitimate Grab at standard rates.' The legitimate fare from Phu Bai Airport (HUI) to central Hue is 150,000–220,000 VND by Grab/Be app or licensed taxi on meter; any quote over 400,000 VND is overcharging. The Dong Hoi-Hue transfer corridor has the same pattern. Community reports document the 2025 Hue transit baseline. Da Nang Airport (DAD) is a common alternative arrival — the Da Nang-Hue 3-hour drive has the same scam-inflation patterns. Reports confirm Grab operates across the corridor, making it the defensive default. For older travelers arriving to Hue, the playbook: (1) book Grab or Be yourself on airport Wi-Fi AFTER you have your luggage — expected fare to central Hue 150K–220K VND; (2) licensed Mai Linh (green, 1055) or Vinasun (1900-1055) taxis are the backup; insist on the meter; (3) walk out of the immediate arrivals hall before booking — scammers concentrate in the first 50 metres; (4) for the Da Nang-Hue 3-hour corridor, pre-book a private car via Klook/12Go at $50–$80 one-way, or take the train (Hue–Da Nang 2.5 hours, 60K VND); (5) REFUSE any driver approaching you inside the arrivals hall offering 'fixed price' transfers. How to avoid: Book Grab or Be yourself on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage pickup Expected fare Phu Bai-central Hue: 150K–220K VND Licensed Mai Linh (green) or Vinasun; insist on meter Walk 50m out of immediate arrivals hall before booking to avoid scammers For Da Nang-Hue, pre-book Klook/12Go car at $50–$80 or train 60K VND

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Perfume River Dragon Boat Tour Pressure (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hue's Perfume River dragon-boat tours are a signature experience but have developed a tourist-pressure pattern. Community reports. Travelers describe a related price-change pattern: 'I had a massage with an agreed-upon discounted price. When I went to pay, the price had changed.' The same mid-service price-change tactic is applied on the dragon-boat route. One 2025 traveler captured the frustration: 'Scams are everywhere man, from street vendors to tour guides, not a good experience.' The Hue-specific patterns: (1) boat operator quotes 200,000 VND at dock, demands 600,000+ VND at end citing 'cultural performance' or 'sunset premium'; (2) 'authentic' singing performance is actually an extra 200K VND supplement not disclosed at booking; (3) mid-river refreshment sales at 3–5x market rate; (4) 'Thien Mu Pagoda stop' promoted as included but actually requires separate cyclo/taxi from the wharf. For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) book the Perfume River tour via a licensed operator (Hue Dragon Boat Tours, hue-dragon-boats.com) with fixed upfront pricing ($15–$25 per person); (2) verify what's included: Thien Mu Pagoda stop, pagoda entry fees, return transfer, performances; (3) refuse mid-river refreshment and performance upsells; (4) for older travelers, the daytime tours (10 AM–3 PM) are significantly less crowded and pressured than sunset tours; (5) tip only at end and only if happy with the service — 50K–100K VND is standard. How to avoid: Book via licensed operator with fixed upfront pricing ($15–$25/person) Verify INCLUSIONS in writing: Thien Mu stop, pagoda entry, return transfer, performances Refuse mid-river refreshment and performance upsells Daytime tours (10 AM–3 PM) are less crowded than sunset tours Tip 50K–100K VND at end only if service was good

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Hue Imperial City Ticket Single-Entry Re-Entry Trap (ticket-fraud, severity: moderate). The Hue Imperial City (Dai Noi / Kinh Thành Huế) has a QR-coded single-entry ticket system that catches tourists who exit for lunch or a bathroom break and then can't re-enter without buying another ticket. One 2025 first-person report notes: 'Unfortunately the ticket is single entry only. That's why they scan the QR code at the entrance.' Tourists who don't know this lose the 200,000 VND ticket and have to pay again for re-entry. The scam isn't fraud per se — it's an undisclosed policy that operates at tourist expense. The variants that compound this: (1) 'guide' outside Dai Noi who sells 'combo tickets' at 2–3x the legitimate rate claiming 'skip the queue'; (2) vendors near the gate selling 'bottled water' at 100K VND (market 15K); (3) motorbike-xe-om drivers offering to 'wait and drive you back' at inflated rates when the legitimate wait time is only 2–3 hours. Travelers describe Hue as awesome: 'It's got a much older feel than Da Nang or Hoi An, and is a center of Vietnam' — confirming Hue is a must-visit, just needs planning. For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) buy the Imperial City ticket at the OFFICIAL ticket booth at Ngọ Môn Gate (Noon Gate) — 200,000 VND adults, 40,000 VND children (2025 rate); the combined ticket with 2 royal tombs (Tu Duc, Minh Mang, or Khai Dinh) is 420,000 VND; (2) enter ONCE and plan a full 3–4 hour visit without exiting; (3) bring your own water, snacks, and lunch OR plan to buy food at the posted-price canteen INSIDE the Imperial City; (4) wear comfortable walking shoes — the site is 2.5 square km; (5) refuse any 'guide' offering combo tickets outside the gate — buy at the official booth; (6) for older travelers, consider a guided tour via Klook/GetYourGuide at $20–$35 per person (includes English-speaking guide, entry ticket, and round-trip transfer). How to avoid: Buy tickets at OFFICIAL booth at Ngọ Môn Gate: 200K VND adult, 420K combined with 2 tombs Enter ONCE — plan 3–4 hour visit without exiting the grounds Bring water and snacks OR use the posted-price canteen INSIDE Refuse 'guides' offering combo tickets outside the gate For guided visits, pre-book via Klook/GetYourGuide at $20–$35/person

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Hue Bicycle Pusher & 'Granddaughter' Guilt Scams (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hue has two documented 2025 street-scam variants targeting older travelers with guilt-based approach. One traveler wrote: 'In Hue, one of those bicycle pushers — I gave him a 500,000 bill and he immediately flashed it into a 20,000 (no change given, claiming no smaller notes).' The scammer pockets the difference and walks. A second 2025 variant: 'I think I got scammed by an older man with a story that his granddaughter was giving lessons.' The 'granddaughter story' leverages emotional sympathy to extract payment for a fake educational cause. The broader pattern: (1) bicycle-cart vendors quote a low price (20,000 VND) but claim to have no change when you hand a 500,000 VND note, pocketing the difference; (2) older men or women with 'granddaughter teaching English' or 'grandson studying medicine' stories demanding donations; (3) children with 'homework' approach seeking payment for signatures or photos; (4) 'flower vendor' giving free flowers then demanding payment. Community reports capture the 2025 cross-Vietnam pattern: 'Scam after scam. Book another hotel, they still got you' — the emotional-pressure scams are part of a broader ecosystem. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) carry small-denomination notes (20K, 50K, 100K) for all street vendor interactions; (2) NEVER hand over a 500K or 200K note to a street vendor — they'll claim no change and pocket it; (3) refuse 'free' gifts from strangers — the request for payment always follows; (4) say 'không' (no) firmly to emotional-pressure stories without engaging; (5) genuine educational or charitable donations in Vietnam go through registered NGOs — street approaches are always scams; (6) for older travelers who feel pressured, walk immediately to the nearest café or hotel lobby. How to avoid: Carry small-denomination notes (20K, 50K, 100K) for street vendors NEVER hand over 500K or 200K VND note to a street vendor — they'll claim no change Refuse 'free' gifts from strangers — payment demand always follows Say 'không' firmly to emotional stories without engaging further If pressured, walk to nearest café or hotel lobby — scammers rarely follow indoors

Scam alert in Hue, Vietnam — Hue Motorbike Tour Rental Damage & 'Scratched Bike' Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Hue is a starting point for the famous 'Hai Van Pass' motorbike route to Hoi An/Da Nang, and the rental-damage-claim scam is documented here similarly to the Lanzarote and Mallorca rental-car patterns. Community reports capture the 2025 fatigue framing. Travelers recommend a specific 5-day luggage-transport operator for the Hue-to-Hoi An Hai Van route. The scam patterns: (1) at return, the shop claims scratches or damage that were present at pickup but weren't documented; (2) fuel-gauge 'not full' claim at return, demanding 100K+ VND refill fee; (3) 'helmet damage' or 'mirror crack' claims; (4) 'insurance upsell' at 2-3x the online rate; (5) hotel-recommended 'local' shops with kickback arrangements and quality issues. Community reports describe the broader Vietnamese-motorbike-rental pattern: breakdown claims are a common post-rental dispute. For older travelers considering a Hai Van Pass motorbike experience, the protective playbook: (1) skip DIY motorbike rental entirely — use an Easy Rider-style operator (Vietnam Easy Riders, Hoi An Easy Riders, OneTrip Hai Van) where you ride pillion with an experienced local rider for $50–$80 per day, includes helmet, insurance, and luggage transport; (2) if you must rent yourself, book via Motorvina, Tigit Motorbikes, or Style Motorbikes (established operators with clear damage-documentation policies, online booking, and English paperwork); (3) at pickup, video a walk-around narrating visible marks (scratches, scuffs, fuel gauge) before signing any paperwork; (4) photograph all sides, seat, mirrors, and tyres; (5) on return, video the vehicle and retain the fuel receipt; (6) for older travelers or those unfamiliar with Vietnamese traffic, an Easy Rider pillion trip is safer than DIY — traffic is intense and road conditions variable. How to avoid: For older travelers, use Easy Rider pillion trips ($50–$80/day) rather than DIY rental For DIY, use Motorvina, Tigit, or Style Motorbikes (established operators) Video walk-around narrating all visible marks at pickup before signing Photograph all sides, seat, mirrors, tyres, and fuel gauge On return, video the vehicle and retain the fuel receipt

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Ijen Crater Mandatory Guide Shakedown at Paltuding Base (tourist-trap, severity: high). Kawah Ijen (2,799m) — the iconic blue-flame volcanic crater with the world's largest acidic turquoise lake — requires a 3-km hike from Paltuding base to the crater rim. Since 2023 the East Java provincial government has officially required a licensed guide for the BLUE FLAME descent (into the crater from the rim to the sulfur-mining level). Community reports document both the regulation and the practical 2024–2025 experience. The 2025 scams at Paltuding: (a) unlicensed 'guides' at the trailhead demanding Rp 300K–500K per person for the crater-rim walk (which does NOT require a guide); the legitimate guide requirement applies ONLY to the blue-flame descent into the crater; (b) legitimate licensed guides charge Rp 200K–350K per group (not per person) for the blue-flame descent; (c) 'entry fee + guide combo Rp 800K' — the real park entry is Rp 150K weekday / Rp 250K weekend per foreigner, guide separate; (d) 'mandatory gas mask Rp 100K rental' — real rate is Rp 30K–50K for a 3M-canister mask; (e) 'compulsory emergency fee Rp 100K' — no such fee exists. Community reports also document the tour-package alternative for those wanting a simpler option. For older travelers — the 3-km 1-hour-each-way crater-rim hike is achievable for moderately fit 60+ travelers; the blue-flame DESCENT (another 700m down into the crater on loose acidic terrain with toxic gas) is NOT recommended above 65 or with ANY heart/lung condition: (1) the crater-rim walk requires NO guide and NO fee beyond park entry; (2) park entry is Rp 150K weekday / Rp 250K weekend per foreigner; (3) if descending to blue flames, a LICENSED guide IS required (check badge, request registration number) — Rp 200K–350K PER GROUP not per person; (4) rent gas mask at Paltuding at Rp 30K–50K — essential for blue-flame descent, recommended for rim; (5) REFUSE all 'mandatory emergency fee' and 'per-person guide' demands at the trailhead; (6) for rim-only visit, arrive at Paltuding 12 AM–1 AM to reach rim for 3–4 AM sunrise; (7) wear sturdy hiking shoes, layers (0–10°C at rim), headlamp with spare batteries; (8) check your travel insurance — Ijen is high-altitude + toxic gas + active volcano, many default policies exclude. How to avoid: Park entry: Rp 150K weekday / Rp 250K weekend per foreigner — that's it Crater-rim walk: NO guide required; descent: yes, Rp 200K–350K PER GROUP Verify licensed guide badge + registration number before paying Rent gas mask at Paltuding at Rp 30K–50K (3M canister type) REFUSE ALL 'emergency fee' and 'per-person guide' demands

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Ijen Gas Mask Rental Overcharge & Fake-Model Fraud (transport, severity: high). Kawah Ijen's crater contains the world's most acidic lake and emits hydrogen sulfide + sulfur dioxide gas — a proper gas mask (3M 6001 canister or equivalent with acid-gas filter) is ESSENTIAL for any descent and strongly recommended for even the crater rim on windward days. Tourists often don't know what 'proper' looks like, creating a 2025 fake-mask and overcharge ecosystem. Community reports document mask preparation requirements and 2025 trip-report experiences. The 2025 scams: (a) Paltuding rentals charging Rp 100K–150K for a 'gas mask' that's actually a N95 surgical mask with a plastic cover — USELESS against H2S; (b) tour packages 'gas mask included' that provide cheap dust masks; (c) 'premium gas mask Rp 300K' claimed to be military-grade — real 3M 6001 + 6000-series full-face rental is Rp 50K–100K; (d) Banyuwangi hotel-lobby rentals at Rp 200K for low-quality masks; (e) 'acid-filter cartridge Rp 150K' surcharge — legitimate rentals include proper cartridges in base fee. For older travelers AND anyone descending to blue flames: (1) CONFIRM the mask is 3M 6000-series (6200, 6800, 7502) half-face or full-face with P100 + acid-gas cartridges — photograph the mask brand/model before accepting rental; reject if anything different; (2) real rental rate at Paltuding is Rp 30K–50K for half-face, Rp 75K–100K for full-face 3M; (3) N95 surgical masks are USELESS against H2S — walk away from any vendor offering one; (4) for serious visitors, buy a proper 3M mask at home before travel (US$20–$35 on Amazon) — more comfortable, guaranteed fit, own hygiene; (5) adjust straps BEFORE entering gas zone — a loose mask is no protection; (6) if wearing glasses, half-face masks work poorly — consider full-face or prescription insert; (7) do NOT descend if you have asthma, COPD, or heart failure even with a mask — gas exposure can be severe; (8) wind direction matters — on leeward days, even rim exposure is unpleasant. How to avoid: Verify 3M 6000-series mask + P100/acid-gas cartridges BEFORE accepting Photograph brand/model before taking; reject anything else Paltuding real rate: Rp 30K–50K half-face, Rp 75K–100K full-face 3M For serious visitors, buy own 3M mask at home (US$20–$35, better fit) Do NOT descend if asthma/COPD/heart failure — even with mask

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Banyuwangi Airport (BWX) & Ferry Terminal Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Banyuwangi is East Java's easternmost city and the launching point for the Kawah Ijen sunrise tour — accessible via Banyuwangi Airport (BWX, small but growing) or via Ketapang ferry from Bali's Gilimanuk port (cheapest Bali-Java connection). The small-city tourism ecosystem creates 2025 taxi-overcharge patterns. The legitimate rates: BWX airport to central Banyuwangi (12 km) is Rp 75K–125K via Grab; Ketapang ferry terminal to central Banyuwangi (5 km) is Rp 40K–75K via Grab; central Banyuwangi to Paltuding base camp (40 km, 1.5 hour mountain drive) is Rp 250K–400K via Grab OR Rp 350K–500K via chartered 4x4 (needed for the steep last 10 km). The 2025 scams: (a) BWX arrivals-kerb taxi kiosks quoting Rp 250K–400K for the 12-km transfer (real Rp 75K–125K); (b) 'direct to Paltuding for Ijen Rp 1.5M' quoted by arrivals touts (real rate Rp 350K–500K); (c) Ketapang ferry touts on the Gilimanuk-Java side offering 'immediate Banyuwangi taxi' at Rp 300K (real Rp 40K–75K); (d) Grab 'doesn't work here' misdirection — Grab IS available throughout Banyuwangi but with 10–15 min wait; (e) unlicensed 4x4 at Paltuding approach with inflated 'mountain premium' at Rp 800K one-way. For older travelers: (1) most Banyuwangi hotels catering to Ijen tourists include free airport transfer with advance booking — USE THIS; (2) if paying, book via hotel or Grab — typical fare BWX-central Rp 75K–125K; Ketapang-central Rp 40K–75K; (3) for central-Banyuwangi-to-Paltuding, arrange via your hotel or Klook at Rp 350K–500K with licensed 4x4 driver (the last 10 km IS steep and needs 4x4); (4) for post-Ijen hike, arrange driver-wait during your trek; (5) IGNORE every airport-kerb kiosk quote above Rp 200K; (6) Grab IS available in Banyuwangi (confirmed 2025) — allow 10–15 min wait; (7) if you're combining Ijen with Bali via Ketapang ferry, the ferry is Rp 10K per foot passenger (5–10 min actual crossing) — no mafia here, just follow the pedestrian lane; (8) most Ijen tours from Bali include the Ketapang ferry and Banyuwangi transfer in package. How to avoid: Use hotel free-transfer on advance booking (most Ijen hotels include) BWX-central via Grab Rp 75K–125K; Ketapang-central Rp 40K–75K For Paltuding transfer, book hotel/Klook at Rp 350K–500K with licensed 4x4 IGNORE every arrivals-kerb quote above Rp 200K Grab IS available throughout Banyuwangi — wait 10–15 min

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Ijen Blue Flame Timing Scam & Late-Arrival 'Just Missed It' Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). The Kawah Ijen blue flames (ignited sulfuric gas at the crater's sulfur-mining level, visible only in pre-dawn darkness) are the reason most tourists visit. Visibility requires: (1) being at the sulfur-mining level BEFORE 4 AM; (2) clear weather; (3) gas masks and guide. The tight timing window creates a 2025 'just missed it' fraud pattern. Community reports document the blue-flame timing logistics. The 2025 scams: (a) tour operators scheduling departure from Banyuwangi at 12 AM (should be 11 PM latest) — deliberately arriving at crater rim after 4 AM (blue flames gone) but charging full 'blue flame tour' price; (b) 'guide' at crater rim claiming 'too late for blue flame' at 3:30 AM and offering 'special descent Rp 500K extra' to recover the experience (real answer: keep walking down, blue flames still visible); (c) group tours that deliberately slow-pace the hike with 'rest stops' to arrive late; (d) 'blue flame guarantee Rp 200K' sold at departure — weather/timing dependent, nothing can guarantee; (e) late refund-refusal — if tourist misses blue flames due to operator lateness, no refund offered. For older travelers AND anyone prioritising blue flames: (1) for blue flames, you MUST be at the sulfur-mining level (crater floor, 700m below rim) BEFORE 4 AM — plan departure from Banyuwangi/Banyuwangi hotel at 10:30 PM–11 PM; (2) reputable operators depart by 11 PM: Sun Tours Ijen, Kawah Ijen Private Tour, Banyuwangi Ijen Adventure; (3) reach Paltuding by 12 AM, start hike 12:15 AM, reach rim by 2:15 AM, descent to blue-flame zone by 3 AM; (4) if your operator is departing after 11 PM, CANCEL and rebook with compliant operator — late departure = no blue flames by physics; (5) REFUSE 'blue flame guarantee' — no operator can guarantee weather; (6) if you miss blue flames, the crater rim at sunrise (5:15 AM) is STILL spectacular (the turquoise acid lake is the daytime highlight); (7) for older travelers who can't descend, rim-only sunrise view is the recommended goal — no blue flames but stunning; (8) allow 3+ hours at Paltuding for the full experience. How to avoid: Depart Banyuwangi by 10:30–11 PM — physics of timing is strict Book Sun Tours Ijen, Kawah Ijen Private Tour, Banyuwangi Ijen Adventure If operator schedules 12 AM departure, CANCEL and rebook compliant REFUSE 'blue flame guarantee' — no operator can guarantee weather If flames missed, sunrise crater rim (5:15 AM) is still spectacular

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Banyuwangi ATM Skimming & Remote Cash-Exchange Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Banyuwangi's rapid Ijen-driven tourism growth has created a 2025 ATM-skimming and cash-exchange-fraud ecosystem that mirrors Bali's pattern in a thinner-monitored environment. Community reports from Bali document the canonical 2025 skimmer patterns; cloned cards from Banyuwangi ATMs are typically used within 1–2 hours at Bali merchants. Community logistics threads also cover Banyuwangi cash-management. The 2025 patterns: (a) freestanding city-center ATMs (not bank-branch) with card-reader overlays + pinhole cameras; (b) hotel-lobby ATMs at tourist Ijen-package hotels from independent operators (not bank-branded) — high-risk; (c) Ketapang ferry terminal cash kiosks with tampered calculators displaying inflated conversion rates; (d) 'no ATM working in town, exchange with me' cover story followed by 8–10% rate padding; (e) rural approach-road ATMs on the Banyuwangi-Paltuding drive — isolated and skimmer-compromised; (f) credit-card surcharge fraud at tour operators: 5–8% 'processing fee' not disclosed at booking. For older travelers: (1) withdraw Rp 2M–4M cash in BALI or at a major Jakarta/Surabaya bank-branch ATM BEFORE travelling to Banyuwangi — this avoids the thinner local ATM risk; (2) if withdrawing in Banyuwangi, use ONLY ATMs INSIDE bank branches (BCA, Mandiri, BNI, BRI) on Jl. Jaksa Agung Suprapto or Jl. MT Haryono during business hours (8 AM–4 PM Mon–Fri); (3) cover keypad when entering PIN; wiggle card slot before inserting; (4) AVOID every freestanding, hotel-lobby, or ferry-terminal ATM; (5) set low daily withdrawal limits (Rp 1.5M–2M) and real-time transaction alerts on your bank app; (6) for cash exchange, use reputable money changer PT Central Kuta or BMC (Bali locations) BEFORE travelling — avoid Banyuwangi hotel-lobby rate padding; (7) CONFIRM credit-card surcharge policy at tour booking in writing — should be 0–3% max; (8) if skimmed, contact your bank IMMEDIATELY via hotel Wi-Fi; file a report at Polres Banyuwangi (+62 333 424 143) for chargeback documentation; (9) keep one dedicated travel debit card separate from main account. How to avoid: Withdraw 3–5 day cash buffer in BALI/Surabaya BEFORE Banyuwangi In Banyuwangi, use ONLY bank-branch ATMs during business hours Cover keypad; wiggle card slot; avoid freestanding/hotel/ferry ATMs Set low daily limits and transaction alerts on bank app Confirm credit-card surcharge (0–3% max) at tour booking in writing

Scam alert in Ijen Crater, Indonesia — Ijen Sulfur-Miner Photo Forced-Tip & Commission Selfie Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Kawah Ijen is one of the world's last active manual sulfur mines — miners carry 70–90 kg sulfur chunks up the steep crater walls by hand twice daily. The dramatic backdrop makes for iconic photographs, and miners SOMETIMES welcome small tips for poses. But a 2025 commission-selfie scam has emerged. Community reports and 2025 trip reports document the pattern. The 2025 scams: (a) 'miner' who's actually an English-speaking tourist-wrangler (not a real miner) posing aggressively and demanding Rp 100K–200K per photo — real miners don't speak English and don't ask; (b) 'photo with real sulfur pole Rp 150K' upsell where the pole is a prop; (c) unofficial 'sulfur souvenir Rp 100K' (small chunk for tourist pocket) — most tour operators don't allow this and proper export is illegal; (d) 'miner donation fundraiser Rp 200K for his family' — well-intentioned tourists over-tip a fake fundraiser; legitimate mining co-op donations go to Ijen Miners Welfare via Banyuwangi hotel front desks; (e) forced-tip for 'carrying your bag' where a 'helpful miner' grabs your backpack then demands Rp 100K at descent. For older travelers: (1) fair-compensation tip for a genuine miner photo is Rp 20K–50K (or a cigarette, traditional small gift) — the mining work is genuinely dangerous + low-paid; (2) REFUSE English-speaking 'miners' demanding Rp 100K+ per photo — real miners are too busy carrying loads and don't speak English; (3) no pole or prop requires a 'fee' — photograph from a respectful distance without commissioning poses; (4) sulfur souvenirs are NOT legal to export (customs will confiscate) and fragment your luggage with sulfurous residue; (5) for genuine support, donate to Ijen Miners Welfare Fund via your Banyuwangi hotel — hotel will take cash donation with receipt, funds tracked; (6) if someone grabs your backpack, firmly say 'saya tidak butuh bantuan' (I don't need help) and take it back — don't engage; (7) photograph miners from a respectful distance — they are working, not posing; (8) the real story: each miner carries 70–90 kg twice daily for ~Rp 100K–150K earnings — your Rp 20K–50K tip is meaningful contribution. How to avoid: Fair miner-photo tip: Rp 20K–50K (or small gift); real miners don't ask REFUSE English-speaking 'miners' quoting Rp 100K+ per photo Don't buy sulfur souvenirs — illegal export + luggage contamination For genuine support, donate to Ijen Miners Welfare via hotel (with receipt) Photograph miners from respectful distance — they are working

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — Ipoh Old Town Unlicensed-Photographer & 'RM800 Photo Fee' Pressure (tourist-trap, severity: high). Ipoh Old Town's heritage zone — Concubine Lane (Lorong Panglima), the Han Chin Pet Soo frontage, the Kinta Riverfront mural wall, the Birch Memorial Clock Tower — has absorbed the national 'unlicensed street photographer' pressure pattern that went viral in July 2025 after Thai tourists at KLCC were charged more than RM800 for roadside photos; SAYS 'Unlicensed Photographers At KLCC Fined RM2,000 Each After Alleged Tourist Scam' (says.com, 2025) is the anchor case, with KL City Hall, police and Immigration issuing compound notices to nearly 30 operators and the federal government publicly confirming NO special permits exist for street-side tourist photography anywhere in Malaysia (Bernama, 2025; NST 'KLCC freelance street photographers fined RM2,000 each', 2025). The same playbook has migrated to Ipoh's 10,000-visitor-a-day heritage lanes per The Star 'From seedy alley to tourist spot' (thestar.com.my, 2024), with community reports providing 2025 traveler baselines. The 2025 mechanic in Ipoh Old Town: (a) a 'freelance photographer' with DSLR and printed lanyard approaches families, couples or solo tourists near Concubine Lane's rainbow-toast stalls or the Mural Art's Lane wall, offering 'one free photo'; (b) after 2-3 shots, a printed RM100–RM300 'package' appears — refusal escalates to RM500–RM800 'session fee' with lanyard-waving and claims of 'Perak tourism permit'; (c) costumed 'vintage cheongsam' or 'concubine' impersonators pose for selfies then demand RM50–RM200 per frame; (d) vendor-side overlay — shop owners claim 'no photo without RM50 minimum purchase' and block exit; (e) 'photographer' follows tourists 50 metres refusing to delete photos until paid; (f) 'scan QR to pay RM80' links to phishing pages per community reports. For travelers: (1) no street-side photographer in Malaysia holds a legal permit — the federal government confirmed this in 2025; you owe them NOTHING for a photo you did not contract in advance; (2) if approached, say firmly 'tidak, terima kasih' and walk — no eye contact, no pose; (3) if photos are taken and a fee demanded, say loudly 'saya nak telefon polis' (I want to call the police) — operators evaporate; (4) for costumed characters, agree a price in writing on your phone BEFORE the photo or refuse; (5) never scan a QR code shown on a stranger's phone — only printed codes on permanent signboards; (6) for genuine heritage photos book Han Chin Pet Soo museum — RM15 admission includes a guided heritage walk; (7) Ipoh Tourist Police (Jalan Sultan Iskandar) speak English: +60 5-253 5522; scam hotline 997; (8) if paid under duress, report to Majlis Bandaraya Ipoh enforcement +60 5-208 3333 within 24 hours — the KLCC 2025 precedent means authorities take these seriously. How to avoid: No Malaysian street-side photographer holds a legal permit — you owe them nothing Walk past; say 'tidak, terima kasih' and do not make eye contact or pose If fee demanded after photos, say 'saya nak telefon polis' — operators evaporate Agree ALL costumed-character prices in writing BEFORE any photo Book official heritage photos via Han Chin Pet Soo museum (RM15) Ipoh Tourist Police English: +60 5-253 5522; national scam line 997

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — AEON Ipoh Station 18 Mall Distraction-Theft (PRC-Linked Ring) (pickpocket, severity: high). Ipoh's busiest shopping-mall pickpocket ring of 2025 was caught on CCTV at AEON Ipoh Station 18 and Ipoh Parade when two women from the People's Republic of China were arrested mid-operation; The Star CCTV coverage 'CCTV footage confirmed that the women made purchases at a number of the malls' (thestar.com.my, 2025) documents the multi-mall pattern. The suspects were confirmed to have worked AEON Ipoh Station 18, Ipoh Parade and Mydin before the arrest, and additional 2025 community reporting shows mall security is actively monitoring. The 2024-2025 ring mechanic: (a) two or three women (often PRC-Mandarin-speaking, well-dressed, carrying branded shopping bags) target women shoppers at the cashier queue of Cold Storage, AEON supermarket or Mydin — one distracts by 'asking for help with product label translation'; (b) second operator reaches into the victim's open handbag, removes purse or phone, passes it to a third walking past; (c) variant near the food court — operator spills water or drops coins on the table, then 'helps clean up' while lifting a phone left beside a handbag; (d) restroom-corridor variant near Ipoh Parade — victim enters stall, operator reaches over the divider for bag hung on the hook; (e) parking-level variant at AEON Ipoh Station 18 — operator bumps victim loading groceries, apologises profusely while partner lifts wallet from handbag; (f) Smart Local Malaysia 2025 reporting (thesmartlocalmy) documents a single Ipoh-mall victim losing RM10,000+ in cash and card fraud after a pickpocket incident at a pedestrian crossing near the mall. Community reports provide a baseline on the rising mall-theft pattern. For travelers: (1) carry a crossbody bag with the zipper side facing your body — NEVER an open tote inside any Malaysian mall; (2) keep phone OFF the food-court table — in your zipped bag between uses; (3) at the cashier queue, keep your bag in FRONT of you with one hand on the zipper — the 'translation help' approach is the tell; (4) anyone spilling water or coins near you at a food court is running the distraction — grab your phone and bag FIRST, accept no help; (5) inside restrooms, hook your bag on the INSIDE of the door or hold between knees — never on the back-of-stall hook; (6) at the parking level, load groceries with your handbag strap across your chest, not on the trolley; (7) if pickpocketed, mall security desks at AEON Ipoh Station 18 (Level G customer service) and Ipoh Parade (Ground floor info counter) will pull CCTV and call Balai Polis Ipoh Timur — +60 5-547 2222; (8) block cards immediately via bank app (Maybank, CIMB, Public Bank all have in-app card-freeze); the PDRM scam-reporting hotline is 997 (CCID) and the Ipoh Tourist Police speak English at +60 5-253 5522. How to avoid: Crossbody bag zipper-side to body; NEVER an open tote in malls Phone OFF food-court tables — in zipped bag between uses At cashier, bag in FRONT with hand on zipper; refuse 'translation help' Spilled water/coins nearby = distraction — grab bag & phone FIRST Block cards in-app via Maybank/CIMB; Balai Polis Ipoh Timur +60 5-547 2222

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — Ipoh 'Macau Scam' Fake-PDRM Phone Impersonation & Bank-Transfer Extortion (tourist-trap, severity: high). The 'Macau scam' — a cold-call impersonation of PDRM officers, Bank Negara officials, customs and couriers — is Malaysia's highest-value fraud category and Ipoh is a 2024-2025 hotspot. The Star 'Ipoh trader loses more than RM1.2 mil to phone scam' (thestar.com.my, via The Star Online Facebook, 2024-2025) is a locally-anchored loss; The Star 'Clerk loses RM445,000 to phone scammers posing as authority figures' (thestar.com.my, 2024) documents a Hutan Melintang (Perak) case with identical script. Community first-person reports and long-running community threads document the same scripts, and Malaysian community wikis on identifying scams. The 2025 mechanic targeting tourists in Ipoh hotels (Weil, M Roof, Kinta Riverfront, Sunway Lost World) and long-stay Airbnbs: (a) cold call in English or Mandarin to the hotel room or mobile — 'this is courier/customs, your parcel from China contains illegal goods'; (b) call is 'transferred' to 'Sergeant Badrul of PDRM Bukit Aman' who cites a fake arrest warrant for money laundering; (c) victim told to stay in the room, not tell anyone, and 'cooperate with the investigation' by transferring savings to a 'Bank Negara safe account' for 'verification'; (d) variant using video call — 'officer' in uniform on WhatsApp with PDRM backdrop demands banking-app screen-share; (e) WhatsApp variant — fake PDRM badge image + case number sent via text, victim pressured to transfer RM50,000–RM500,000+ in tranches; (f) tourist-specific hook — 'your hotel check-in triggered an immigration flag, you must clear RM5,000 bond to a verification account or face deportation' per 2025 community reports. PDRM's official Facebook (pdrmsiaofficial, 2024-2025) confirms over RM500 million lost to phone scammers in recent years. For travelers: (1) no legitimate Malaysian agency — PDRM, Bank Negara, Immigration, Customs, JPJ — will EVER cold-call you, demand money, ask for bank details, or threaten deportation by phone; (2) if called, HANG UP — do not 'press 9' or stay on the line 'to be transferred'; (3) PDRM will never accept payment by bank transfer; real fines are written, paid at a police station with a serialised receipt; (4) NEVER share bank OTPs, PINs, card numbers or screen-share banking apps — not with 'police', 'hotel front desk calling back' or anyone; (5) if an Ipoh hotel room phone rings and the caller claims authority, put the call on hold, walk to the front desk, and verify in person — real authorities will come to the hotel, they don't phone; (6) call the Malaysian National Scam Response Centre directly: 997 (24/7, English available); verify with PDRM Perak HQ +60 5-208 6222; (7) Ipoh Tourist Police (Jalan Sultan Iskandar) +60 5-253 5522 speaks English; (8) if you have already transferred money, call 997 immediately — the first 24-48 hours is the only window to trace and freeze; block your bank cards in-app (Maybank, CIMB, Public Bank freeze buttons) before calling the bank. How to avoid: NO Malaysian agency will cold-call demanding money or bank details HANG UP — do not 'press 9' or accept call transfers NEVER share OTP, PIN, card numbers or screen-share banking apps Verify in person at hotel front desk if room phone rings Malaysian Scam Hotline 997 (24/7 English); PDRM Perak +60 5-208 6222 If money transferred, call 997 within 24 hours and freeze cards in-app

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — Concubine Lane (Lorong Panglima) Tourist-Trap Overcharge & Instagram-Trap Vendors (food, severity: moderate). Concubine Lane (Lorong Panglima) is Ipoh Old Town's single most-hyped tourist strip — The Star 'From seedy alley to tourist spot' (thestar.com.my, 2024) reports up to 10,000 visitors daily across three heritage lanes and roughly 50 shophouses — and the 2024-2025 pricing drift has turned a historically cheap lane into a 3-5x mark-up food-and-souvenir trap. Long-running community threads document the pattern, with 2025 first-person reports on Old Town pricing fatigue and 2025 traveler baselines providing supporting coverage. The 2025 overcharge pattern: (a) 'hand-pulled old-town white coffee' at RM12–RM18 a cup when the authentic Ipoh Old Town kopitiam rate is RM3.50–RM6 (Sin Yoon Loong, Nam Heong, Thean Chun just 200 metres away); (b) 'Instagram rainbow cheese toast' RM20 per slice plus a mandatory RM8 drink (Star 2024); (c) pomelo and nut stalls — RM30–RM60 per bag of mixed nuts that cost RM10 at Ipoh Parade; (d) costumed 'concubine' selfie-hawkers asking RM20–RM50 per photo after posing; (e) 'heritage egg tart' vendors charging RM8 each when the local Restoran Foh San or Sin Eng Heong price is RM2.50; (f) weekend-only surcharge — some stalls add 'RM5 sitting fee' or 'QR-code scan to order' that loads a minimum spend; (g) credit-card surcharge — vendors quoting in cash then adding 5-10% 'bank fee' to card payments, often not disclosed. Community reports from KL show the same playbook in adjacent tourist zones. For travelers: (1) walk ONE block out of Concubine Lane to Jalan Bandar Timah for real Ipoh Old Town kopitiam prices — Sin Yoon Loong, Nam Heong, Thean Chun are RM3.50–RM6 for white coffee, RM3–RM5 for kaya toast; (2) for egg tarts, Sin Eng Heong (Jalan Mustapha Al-Bakri) and Foh San (Jalan Osborne) are RM2–RM3 each; (3) ALWAYS ask price BEFORE ordering at any Concubine Lane stall — the 'bao' (packaged) price is typically posted, the 'special' tourist add-ons are not; (4) refuse any QR-code order menu at a street stall — pay cash and ask for a written receipt; (5) for costumed photos, agree the price in writing (type on your phone, show them, they nod) or skip — expect RM5–RM15 per photo at most; (6) card surcharges over 2% should be reported to Bank Negara (bnmlink@bnm.gov.my); (7) the genuine heritage experience is Han Chin Pet Soo museum (Jalan Bijeh Timah) RM15, advance booking at ipohworld.org — it is far richer than Concubine Lane's lane of Instagram props; (8) save the MBI Tourism hotline +60 5-208 3333 for price-gouging complaints and Tripadvisor 'Incident on first night - Ipoh Forum' community threads for ongoing scam reports near the lane. How to avoid: Walk one block to Jalan Bandar Timah for real kopitiam RM3.50–RM6 Sin Eng Heong & Foh San egg tarts RM2–RM3 (not RM8 lane rate) ASK price BEFORE ordering; refuse QR-code menus; pay cash with receipt Agree costumed-photo prices in writing or skip (expect RM5–RM15 max) Han Chin Pet Soo museum RM15 = real heritage experience MBI Tourism hotline +60 5-208 3333; Bank Negara bnmlink@bnm.gov.my for surcharges

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — Fake Traffic-Police Document-Check & Cash Shakedown in Ipoh (transport, severity: moderate). Ipoh's fake-traffic-police shakedown pattern produced a landmark 2025 conviction — Malay Mail 'Two men fined RM5,000 each for impersonating traffic police, demanding money from teens in Ipoh' (malaymail.com, 2025-11-04), New Straits Times 'Two men fined RM5,000 each for impersonating police' (nst.com.my, 2025), The Star 'Duo fined RM5,000 each for impersonating cops' (thestar.com.my, 2025) and Bernama 'Two Friends Fined RM10,000 For Impersonating Traffic Police' (bernama.com, 2025) all cover the same Ipoh Magistrates' Court ruling. The convicted pair stopped victims at 12:38 AM on Jalan Lebuh Bercham Selatan 1 and Tong Seng Street wearing 'uniforms resembling traffic police including cream-striped black trousers', threatened summonses over 'modified motorcycles' and extracted a RM400 bank transfer; Wong Jiun Wei (24) was caught with a genuine PDRM cap and JSPT boots and fined an additional RM2,000. Community reports document the reaction. Tripadvisor 'Incident on first night - Ipoh Forum' (tripadvisor.com) is a long-running community thread with a Perth traveler's near-miss involving three men in a grey SUV with a PDRM card but no photo. The 2025 pattern affecting tourists: (a) two men in matching dark-blue or black polo shirts with printed 'PDRM' or 'JSPT' flash approach pedestrians, motorcyclists or cyclists on Old Town side-streets (Jalan Masjid, Jalan Sultan Iskandar, Jalan Bercham); (b) demand to see passport/IC and driving license, then 'find' an infraction (no helmet, wrong-way one-way, 'modified vehicle'); (c) offer to 'settle on the spot' for RM200–RM500 cash instead of RM2,000+ summons or arrest; (d) variant with a genuine PDRM cap (stolen or bought online) to create authenticity; (e) e-wallet / QR-code payment demand (DuitNow QR) which moves money instantly to a mule account; (f) late-night Old Town bar-exit targeting — tourists leaving Concubine Lane bars after 10 PM singled out. Critically, genuine Malaysian traffic police (JSPT) NEVER accept cash on the spot — all fines are written (Form POL 257) and paid at any police station, balai polis, Pos Malaysia, or via the JPJ/MyBayar Saman app. For travelers: (1) ask politely 'boleh saya lihat warrant card?' (may I see your warrant card?) — genuine PDRM have a laminated photo-ID card; a card without photo is fake per Tripadvisor 2016 community reporting and the 2025 Malay Mail conviction; (2) NEVER pay cash on the spot — say 'saya nak bayar di balai polis' (I want to pay at the police station); genuine officers will accept this; (3) NEVER scan any QR code offered by an officer — real fines are NOT paid by QR to an individual; MyBayar Saman is the only legitimate app; (4) show a laminated photocopy of your passport — never surrender the original; (5) ask for their name, rank, and PDRM ID number and WRITE IT DOWN on your phone in front of them — fake officers bail; (6) if you feel unsafe, say 'saya nak telefon konsulat saya dan 999' (I want to call my consulate and 999) — 999 is the Malaysian police emergency number; (7) Ipoh Tourist Police (Jalan Sultan Iskandar) +60 5-253 5522 speak English; PDRM Perak HQ +60 5-208 6222; (8) if shaken down, file a report at the nearest balai polis within 24 hours for possible refund and prosecution — the November 2025 convictions show Perak courts are actively prosecuting. How to avoid: Ask 'boleh saya lihat warrant card?' — real PDRM have PHOTO-ID card NEVER pay cash on the spot — say 'saya nak bayar di balai polis' NEVER scan a QR code offered by an officer — real fines are not paid this way Show passport photocopy only; write down badge number in front of them Emergency: 999; Ipoh Tourist Police +60 5-253 5522 (English)

Scam alert in Ipoh, Malaysia — Cave Temple & Gua Tempurung 'Guide / Parking / Donation' Tout Overcharge (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Ipoh's four flagship cave attractions — Kek Lok Tong, Sam Poh Tong, Perak Tong (all free-entry Buddhist cave temples) and Gua Tempurung (official RM22 limestone-cave tour) — are 2024-2025 tout zones where unofficial 'guides', 'parking attendants' and 'donation collectors' extract RM50–RM200+ from tourists who do not realize entry is free or that official tours are cheap. Tripadvisor 'Entrance fee is not equal to donation - Review of Perak Tong Cave Temple' (tripadvisor.com) documents the pattern; Tripadvisor 'Kek Lok Tong Cave Temple and Zen Gardens' FAQ confirms the temples are free. Community reports and 2025 traveler baselines provide supporting coverage. The 2024-2025 mechanic: (a) at Perak Tong (Jalan Kuala Kangsar), men in yellow safety vests wave tourists into 'VIP parking' for RM20–RM50 when the temple's own lot is free and 20 metres further; (b) unofficial 'English-speaking guide' intercepts at the entrance offering '30-min tour' at RM100–RM200 per person — the free signage already covers the content; (c) at Sam Poh Tong (Jalan Gopeng), a 'donation collector' with a clipboard demands 'RM50 maintenance fee' — the temple has a voluntary donation box inside, no fee at entry; (d) at Kek Lok Tong (Gunung Rapat), touts at the pond demand RM10 per pellet bag for 'fish feeding' (RM1 elsewhere); (e) at Gua Tempurung (Gopeng, 25 km south), unofficial guides at the car park offer 'full 2.5-hour adventure' at RM150–RM250 per person when the official Jabatan Mineral dan Geosains counter charges RM22 Tour 1 (40-min dry walk) and RM33–RM66 for full wet-dry tours with certified guide; (f) 'taxi-tour' combo — a Grab or unofficial driver offers 'all four caves for RM350' then pockets the touts' commission. Community reports warn about the cave-tout ecosystem. For travelers: (1) Kek Lok Tong, Sam Poh Tong and Perak Tong are ALL FREE — any gate fee or 'mandatory donation' is a scam; give voluntarily into the clearly-marked box inside if you wish; (2) Gua Tempurung's ONLY legitimate ticket counter is the Jabatan Mineral dan Geosains office at the cave entrance — RM22/33/44/66 per tour level, certified guide included; (3) refuse 'VIP parking' — temples and Gua Tempurung have free official parking 20–50 metres past the touts; (4) refuse unofficial 'guide' intercepts — temples are self-guided with English signage; arrange through Tourism Perak +60 5-255 2772 if needed; (5) decline 'fish-feeding' and 'incense' upsells at the entry; (6) book cave tours via Ipoh Tourist Information Centre or a MOTAC-licensed operator; (7) Grab fares from Ipoh city: Perak Tong RM15–RM25, Kek Lok Tong RM20–RM30, Gua Tempurung RM60–RM80 one-way — never accept off-meter 'combo' quotes; (8) report tout harassment to Tourism Perak +60 5-255 2772 or 999. How to avoid: Kek Lok Tong, Sam Poh Tong, Perak Tong are FREE — any gate fee is a scam Gua Tempurung official counter: RM22 Tour 1, RM33–RM66 full tours Refuse 'VIP parking' — free lots are 20–50 metres past the touts No unofficial 'English guide' — temples are self-guided with English signs Grab flat fare from city: Perak Tong RM15–RM25, Gua Tempurung RM60–RM80 Tourism Perak +60 5-255 2772; emergency 999

Scam alert in Jakarta, Indonesia — Jakarta Soekarno-Hatta Airport (CGK) Taxi Overcharge & Airport Sharks (transport, severity: high). Soekarno-Hatta Airport (CGK) has one of Southeast Asia's most-documented 2025 tourist-taxi overcharge problems. Community reports document the pattern: drivers approach at arrivals offering 'premium' or 'VIP' rides quoting fixed prices 4–8x the legitimate Blue Bird or Grab rate. The 2025 community baseline confirms Grab and Gojek are the ONLY reliable price-transparent options for foreigners at CGK. The specific Terminal 3 pattern: 'sharks' wearing hotel-uniform-style polos wait past the customs exit, approach Western tourists and say 'Taxi, sir? Grab not allowed here, I take you.' They walk the tourist to a parking-level unmarked sedan and then charge 500K–1.5M IDR (US$30–$95) to Kuningan, Menteng, or South Jakarta — the legitimate Blue Bird meter or Grab rate is 150K–250K IDR (US$10–$16). A separate variant operates at the 'Premium Taxi' kiosks that are real but heavily overpriced (450K–700K flat) and marketed as 'safer'. Community reports document that even regular-looking taxi queues sometimes stage 'broken meter' routines then demand cash-only large bills. For older travelers, the defensive protocol: (1) ignore EVERY approach inside the terminal and in the covered walkway — all official pickup happens outdoors at the clearly-signposted Blue Bird Group counter or the Grab/Gojek pickup zones (look for 'Grab Lounge' signs); (2) book Grab or Gojek yourself on airport Wi-Fi AFTER collecting luggage and verify license plate; (3) if using metered taxi, insist ONLY on Blue Bird (bright blue, 'Blue Bird' logo, not just any blue car) or Silver Bird (black, premium-metered); (4) legitimate fare CGK to central Jakarta is 150K–250K IDR via Grab, 200K–300K via metered Blue Bird; NEVER accept 'fixed price' quotes; (5) request a receipt (bukti); real drivers will issue one instantly via the app or a printed slip. How to avoid: Use Grab or Gojek app booked on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage; verify license plate For metered taxi, insist ONLY on Blue Bird (bright blue) or Silver Bird (black) — outdoor queue Typical fare CGK to central Jakarta: 150K–250K IDR Grab, 200K–300K Blue Bird IGNORE every 'taxi sir' approach inside terminal — all official pickup is outdoors Refuse 'Premium Taxi' kiosks and cash-only fixed-price quotes

Scam alert in Jakarta, Indonesia — Jakarta Blue Bird Taxi Impersonator & Meter Tampering (transport, severity: high). Jakarta has a long-running 2025 Blue Bird IMPERSONATOR problem — blue-painted non-Blue-Bird taxis with near-identical logos and 'Blue Bird' or 'Blue Bird Taxi' stickers that are not affiliated with the legitimate Blue Bird Group. Community reports document how tourists routinely mistake any blue-painted car for the real thing.
